serious_errors.materiality: The report places paragraph 5's joint-tenure and kinship-based revenue arrangement under the 1861 agreement, although the supplied settlement sequence locates that paragraph in the later 1877 settlement discussion. The distinction matters to the historical development of proprietary rights, the relationship between Dalmir's early sole-owner records and subsequent joint-ownership evidence, and the chronology of settlement restrictions. The underlying paragraph 5 content is accurate, but its documentary attribution is materially wrong.

important_omissions.omission: The original grant's disputed proprietary scope and the early sole-owner documentary evidence are insufficiently developed. Dalmir claimed sole-grantee status with full proprietary rights, the initial settlement described him as sole owner, and some early records were lost.

source_evidence.quote: Dalmir claimed to be the sole grantee with full proprietary rights.

important_omissions.materiality: These details establish the historical foundation and evidentiary limitations of the Dalmir branch's exclusive-title theory.

important_omissions.omission: The report does not mention that the 1861 document was verified by individuals from the other branches who were described as proprietors, notwithstanding the distinction between village-wide profits and rights to cultivated produce.

source_evidence.quote: This document is signed in token of verification by Dalmir Lamberdar, 64 Dilmor, Alif Khan Biswadar and Phusa Biswadar, who ,ire described as proprietors.

important_omissions.materiality: The description of other signatories as proprietors complicates an inference that produce-only rights necessarily excluded proprietary standing.

important_omissions.omission: The report omits the affirmative 1877 settlement history that Dalmir took possession together with his brothers, other branches subsequently joined, the parties described themselves as joint owners, and the village had never been partitioned.

source_evidence.quote: Dalmir, Caste Meo, Got Sogan, along with Dilmor and Chhinga, his real brothers, took possession of the area of this village
He along with his brothers jointly remained in possession thereof and enjoyed profit and bore loss.
We have up to this day been joint owners. This village has never been partitioned. Shares are given in the Khewat papers.

important_omissions.materiality: This provides affirmative historical support for common proprietary rights and explains the later joint-tenure settlement record. It is distinct from merely recording equal possession.

important_omissions.omission: The report does not separately reconstruct the express 1903–08 Wajib-ul-arz provision allowing Dalmir's descendants to seek partition into five shares while denying that facility to the other four branches because of the stated accounting and revenue arrangements.

main_answer_reason: The report gives a substantial, predominantly source-supported reconstruction of the opposing ownership and possession claims, the original grant's documentary uncertainty, the 1861 agreement, equal-share revenue and possession entries, Mehrab's testimony, the 1893 Chief Court litigation, and the later trial and High Court findings. It correctly preserves the distinction between prior adjudications and the withheld target disposition, and identifies the adverse-possession submission as unresolved in the permitted view. Its principal confirmed substantive defect is the placement of the 1877 paragraph 5 joint-tenure and revenue arrangement under the 1861 agreement, which materially distorts the settlement chronology. It also omits important evidence supporting the competing title theories, especially the affirmative 1877 joint-ownership history, the specific 1903–08 partition restriction, earlier adverse-possession and Bhandadar pleadings, the basis of the 1893 decree, and the unchallenged sale testimony. The description of a statutory partition right and the precise identification of the target appellate institution are not independently established by the allowed view, but neither is sufficient here to make the entire substantive answer wrong. The appropriate assessment is therefore PARTIAL, without inferring any withheld final result.
